significance: Vadiraja opens the western circuit by describing the land Parashurama reclaimed from the sea and gifted to Brahmins: the coast from Gokarna to Kanyakumari is Parashurama Kshetra, framing the whole western seaboard as sacred.
nearest_railway_station: Region (served along its length by the Konkan Railway)
how_to_reach: Coastal belt; Konkan Railway runs its length between Mangaluru and points north/south.

significance: The sacred temple tank adjoining the Sri Krishna temple at Udupi, described for its purifying power for pilgrims.
how_to_reach: In Udupi town, beside the Krishna temple; ~60 km north of Mangaluru.

also_known_as: Rajata Peetha Kshetra, Udupi Krishna Matha
significance: Vadiraja glorifies the Krishna idol that (per tradition) came from Dwaraka by ship and was rescued by Madhvacharya during a storm and installed at Udupi, worshipped in rotation by the eight mathas. As an ashta-matha pontiff, this is Vadiraja's central kshetra.
how_to_reach: Udupi town centre; ~60 km from Mangaluru, ~95 km from Mangaluru airport.

significance: An ancient Udupi shrine where Madhvacharya's father served as priest; on moving to Pajaka he carried a replica of Ananta-Padmanabha.
how_to_reach: Adjacent to the Sri Krishna temple complex, Udupi.

significance: The birthplace of Madhvacharya, surrounded by four theerthas said to be created by Parashurama — Parasu, Dhanus, Gada and Bana Teertha.
how_to_reach: ~13 km south-east of Udupi town by road.

modern_name: Kunjarugiri Durga temple hill, near Udupi
significance: A hilltop Durga shrine near Udupi, traditionally consecrated by Parashurama.
how_to_reach: Near Pajaka, ~11–13 km from Udupi.

significance: Noted for its special Rudrakshi-shila linga; tradition holds the temple door opened on its own for Vadiraja's darshan.
how_to_reach: On the outskirts of Mangaluru.

deity: Shaligrama (one of eight Madhvacharya brought from Badari)
significance: Madhvacharya's midday worship halt en route from Udupi to Subrahmanya, housing one of the eight Badari shaligramas.
how_to_reach: On the road between Udupi and Kukke Subrahmanya.

modern_name: Chintamani Narasimha, near the Nethravathi (Mangaluru region)
significance: When demonic forces disturbed Shiva's penance, Narasimha rose from Patala, destroyed them and protected Shiva — hence this shrine on the Nethravathi bank.
how_to_reach: On the Nethravathi riverbank near Mangaluru/Bantwal.

significance: The Nethravathi and its confluence with the Kumaradhara are praised as purifying river-tirthas of the western coast.
how_to_reach: Confluence at Uppinangady, on the Mangaluru–Subrahmanya road.

significance: A holy river near Kukke Subrahmanya, praised as a distinct tirtha (separate from the Netravati described just before it); pilgrims bathe in it to purify themselves before the darshan of Subrahmanya.
how_to_reach: Flows at Kukke Subrahmanya; ~7 km from Subrahmanya Road station.

significance: Set in the Sahyadri forests; visiting clears past sins and is held efficacious for curing skin diseases and ailments. Also linked to the Vedavyasa Samputa (a hidden shaligrama shrine).
how_to_reach: ~7 km from Subrahmanya Road station; ~105 km from Mangaluru.

significance: The Payaswini flowing by Subrahmanya is glorified as a sacred river-tirtha.
how_to_reach: Flows near Kukke Subrahmanya.

significance: Named among the sacred western river-tirthas.
how_to_reach: Near Udupi.

significance: The demon Kumbhasura was defeated here; because Bhima slew the demon with a sword (asi), the place became Kumbhashi.
how_to_reach: ~30 km north of Udupi, near Kundapura.

significance: A crore (koti) of sages worshipped Shiva here, so it became Kotee-eshwara, later Koteshwara.
how_to_reach: ~2 km from Kumbhashi, near Kundapura.

significance: One of the Sapta-Mahakshetras of Parashurama's Tulunadu, on the Shuktimati (Souparnika) river near Koteshwara; the text names it 'Kroda'. A naturally-formed (udbhava) linga sits a foot below ground, with the Shankara linga on the right and the Narayana linga on the left — its modern town is Shankaranarayana.
how_to_reach: Inland from Kundapura in Udupi district.

significance: Devi Shakti descended and slew the demon Mookasura, from which the goddess is named Mookambika.
how_to_reach: ~80 km from Udupi at the foot of the Kodachadri hills.

significance: The Sahyadri range is praised as the sacred mountain-tirtha of the western region.
how_to_reach: The ghat ranges paralleling the Karnataka coast.

deity: Harihara — Shiva and Vishnu combined in one idol
significance: On the banks of the Tungabhadra; Hari and Hara are seen together in a single idol in the sanctum.
how_to_reach: Harihar town on the Tungabhadra, on the Bengaluru–Hubballi line.

significance: The ashwattha-Narayana shrine on the Tungabhadra bank; its blessings are said to equal distant pilgrimages.
how_to_reach: On the Tungabhadra riverbank.

significance: A Shiva shrine on the Tungabhadra bank praised alongside the Ashwatha Narayana shrine.
how_to_reach: On the Tungabhadra riverbank.

significance: By tradition the Pandavas stayed here after escaping the lac palace and consecrated this Keshava idol.
how_to_reach: Bankapura, ~25 km from Haveri.

significance: Named as a sacred river-tirtha of the region (flows near Banavasi).
how_to_reach: Flows through Haveri / Uttara Kannada districts near Banavasi.

significance: The very ancient (Kadamba-era) temple at Banavasi.
how_to_reach: ~25 km from Sirsi.

significance: Praised as sin-purifying waters.
how_to_reach: Near Sonda / Sirsi.

significance: Noted for its special (seasonal) properties as a sacred river.
how_to_reach: Near Sirsi, Uttara Kannada.

deity: Sri Trivikrama (idol brought by Vadiraja); Vadiraja's Brindavana
significance: Vadiraja's own principal seat, where he installed the Trivikrama idol brought from Badari. The site has a unique three-wheeled stone chariot, one wheel used to defeat a demon during construction.
how_to_reach: ~20 km from Sirsi.

significance: The name Manjuguni is said to derive from the thick winter fog covering the place.
how_to_reach: ~26 km from Sirsi.

significance: The cave-sanctuary Bhairava shrine among the western tirthas at Yana.
how_to_reach: Yana rocks, in the Sahyadri near Kumta/Sirsi.

significance: Ravana carried the Atmalinga and Ganesha tricked him into setting it down permanently, after which Shiva here became Mahabaleshwara.
how_to_reach: ~10 km from Gokarna Road station; on the Konkan coast north of Kumta.

significance: The very ancient gemstone idol of Mahalakshmi, who resides at Kolhapur after leaving Vaikuntha over Brihaspati's offence.
how_to_reach: Kolhapur city, southern Maharashtra.

significance: Praised as a sin-cleansing river of western India.
how_to_reach: Crosses Maharashtra/Gujarat, meeting the sea near Surat.

significance: Glorified as among the holiest rivers of the western circuit.
how_to_reach: Flows across central-western India to the Gulf of Khambhat.

significance: The site of the first jyotirlinga, where Chandra built a golden temple and installed the glorious Jyotirlinga.
how_to_reach: ~6 km from Veraval on the Saurashtra coast.

significance: The spring arose where Krishna, struck in the foot by the hunter Jara's arrow, drew it out — the Bana (arrow) Ganga.
how_to_reach: Near Somnath / Prabhasa.

significance: Krishna's western capital, built after defeating Kushasura, said to have submerged after his avatar's mission.
how_to_reach: Dwarka town on the western tip of Saurashtra.

significance: The Gomati merges with the sea at Dwaraka and daily washes the feet of Dwarakanatha.
how_to_reach: At Dwarka, where the river meets the Arabian Sea.

significance: Where the Chakra Tirtha merges into the sea, ordinary stones turn into chakrankita stones fit for worship like shaligramas.
how_to_reach: Near Dwarka on the coast.

significance: This island tirtha is associated with Krishna's victory over the demon Panchajanya (from whom the conch Panchajanya came).
how_to_reach: Island off Okha, ~30 km from Dwarka, reached by boat.

significance: Those who wear the gopichandana clay from here are said to become spiritually powerful and more knowledgeable.
how_to_reach: Near Dwarka.

significance: Siddhapuri bestows moksha, and Bindusarovara originates from the compassionate tears of Kapila.
how_to_reach: Siddhpur town, northern Gujarat.

significance: The concluding place of the western section: Vishnu remained here as Varaha after slaying Hiranyaksha, and the lake formed where Brahma's lotus (pushkara) fell, making it a supreme (tirtharaja) pilgrimage site.
nearest_railway_station: Ajmer Junction (Pushkar has a small halt)
how_to_reach: ~11–15 km from Ajmer.

significance: The Krishnaveni (confluence of Krishna and Veni) removes the sins of crores of births even by mere darshana; the commentary notes the river is treated grammatically as masculine because Lord Krishna Himself is present within it. It opens the Uttara section.
nearest_railway_station: Wai/Satara or Sangli (upper Krishna sangama points)
how_to_reach: Sacred confluence points along the Krishna in western Maharashtra; reach by road from Satara/Sangli.

deity: Panduranga / Vittala (Vithoba), a form of Vishnu
significance: Vadiraja praises the Vittala icon on the Bhimarathi (Chandrabhaga), reading its posture (hands on the waist, un-adorned) as signifying detachment and assurance of protection from samsara. A punya-kshetra revered by the Haridasa tradition.
how_to_reach: Rail to Pandharpur/Solapur; road from Solapur and Pune.

modern_name: Godavari River (source at Trimbak, near Nashik)
deity: Ganga/Godavari (river goddess); linked to sage Gautama
significance: Ranked among India's seven great rivers, second only to the Ganga, originating at Tryambaka hill near Nashik from the episode of sage Gautama obtaining Ganga-water to revive a cow; it grants merit and bhakti to Krishna, and liberation.
nearest_railway_station: Nashik Road (for the Trimbak source / Panchavati)
how_to_reach: Rail to Nashik Road; road to Trimbakeshwar (source) and Panchavati ghats.

deity: Yamuna Devi (sister of Yama); linked to Krishna's realm
significance: The Yamuna purifies sinful devotees and, through her affection, ensures her devotees attain Shvetadvipa in the Ocean of Milk rather than any lesser destination.
how_to_reach: Reachable at Mathura, Delhi and Prayagraj (Triveni) by rail and road.

significance: The Triveni confluence of Ganga, Yamuna and (subterranean) Saraswati is the supreme tirtha; remembrance of Veni Madhava equals an excellent yaga. The commentary calls the Triveni 'a pair of scissors for heaps of sin.'
how_to_reach: Well connected by rail and air; Triveni Sangama reached by road/boat within the city.

deity: Ganga Devi; originates from Vishnu's feet
significance: The Ganga originates from the foot of Vishnu as Trivikrama, is collected by Brahma, descends onto Rudra's head and reaches earth through Bhagiratha's tapas; flowing through the three worlds, bathing in and devotion to her destroys sin and grants liberation.
how_to_reach: Accessible at numerous ghats along its course by rail and road.

significance: Among the seven moksha-puris, housing Bindu Madhava and Vishwanatha; constantly resolving 'I will go to Kashi' earns merit. The commentary presents Rudra here as a supreme devotee of Vishnu, and Kashi (between the Asi and Varana) as ideal for one's final days.
how_to_reach: Well connected by rail and air; ghats and temples within the city.

significance: Vishnu resides at Gaya as Gadadhara and the Vishnupada marks where the Lord placed His foot on the dharma-stone. Performing shraddha once at Gaya, by the Phalgu, is said to redeem forefathers and negate the karma of many lifetimes.
how_to_reach: Rail and air (Gaya airport); Vishnupada temple and Phalgu ghats within the city.

significance: The avatara-kshetra where Krishna was born; good deeds done here destroy sin and the influence of Kali. The commentary pictures the city as guarded by detached devotees as its army and the Lord's name as its fortress.
how_to_reach: Well connected by rail and road on the Delhi–Agra corridor.

deity: Sri Krishna (childhood leelas with the gopis)
significance: The exceptionally holy forest of Krishna's boyhood sports with the gopis, fragrant and radiant with divine trees; the name is derived from the tapas of Vrunda, daughter of King Kedara.
nearest_railway_station: Mathura Junction (nearest major); Vrindavan town station
how_to_reach: Road from Mathura (~12 km); rail via Mathura Junction.

significance: 'Resplendent like a chaste wife,' one of the seven moksha-puris; even during Rama's exile the city honoured His wooden sandals as His presence. Commentators note Vadiraja visited soon after the 1528 destruction of the Rama temple.
how_to_reach: Rail to Ayodhya/Faizabad; road and air (Ayodhya airport).

deity: Vishnu; site of the sages' sattra
significance: A supreme sacred forest where 'the story of Krishna is like a creeper grown in the hearts of the great rishis' — where Suta narrated the Bhagavata and Puranas to Shaunaka and the assembled sages.
how_to_reach: Rail to Sandila/Sitapur then road; road from Lucknow (~90 km).

significance: Its significance rests on the Pandavas' establishment of dharma, especially Bhima's valour defeating the Kaurava forces; the Pandavas ruled 36 years after the war and performed the Ashwamedha yaga.
how_to_reach: Road from Meerut (~35 km); nearest rail at Meerut.

significance: The battlefield where Bhimasena's mace ground the enemy hosts to pieces — the ground where the Bhagavad Gita and Vishnu Sahasranama were delivered and where Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows; an enduring seat of dharma, renowned for eclipse-time bathing.
how_to_reach: Rail on the Delhi–Ambala line; road via NH-44.

significance: The prophesied birthplace of Kalki, 'the one who will destroy the strength of Kali'; pilgrimage here is presented as a means to overcome the corrupting influence of the Kali age.
how_to_reach: Rail to Chandausi/Sambhal; road from Moradabad.

modern_name: Prayaga, Vishnuprayag, Devprayag, Rudraprayag, Skandaprayag, Karnaprayag (Alaknanda confluences)
deity: Ganga confluences (Vishnu forms at each prayag)
significance: The six prayagas from the main Prayaga up to the Bhima-setu at Badarinath; the commentary makes their turbulent waters a metaphor for uprooting the six inner enemies (kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya) and cleansing sin.
how_to_reach: Rail to Haridwar/Rishikesh, then road along the Alaknanda/Ganga toward Badarinath.

significance: 'The spiritual capital of Bharata-khanda,' used to establish Narayana's supremacy. The Alakananda flows here; nearby Vasudhara falls is where Hayagriva appeared at Brahma's sacrifice; caves of Vyasa and Ganesha are noted. This is the last place of the Uttara section.
how_to_reach: Rail to Rishikesh/Haridwar, then road (~295 km) via Devprayag–Joshimath.

modern_name: Hidden Himalayan region north of Vishala Badari
deity: Narayana; abode of Veda Vyasa and Sri Madhwacharya
significance: Distinguished from the commonly-visited Vishala Badari: a further-north Uttara Badari 'where Lord Veda Vyasa and Sri Madhwacharya reside even today,' revered as an inaccessible divine ashrama rather than an ordinary pilgrimage stop.
how_to_reach: Described as a hidden region beyond Badarinath, not reachable as a normal pilgrimage destination.

deity: Kapila / Ganga (Ganga's confluence with the sea)
significance: Citing Madhwacharya's Mahabharata Tatparya Nirnaya, this is where the Ganga merges into the Bay of Bengal; the commentary ties it to the story of Varuna's curse. It opens the eastern circuit.
how_to_reach: Rail to Kakdwip/Namkhana from Kolkata, then road to Lot-8/Harwood Point and ferry to Sagar Island.

significance: One of the four celebrated kshetras of Bharata; the wooden murtis were fashioned by Vishwakarma from a log found in the sea. Vadiraja uses the shrine to stress tattvavada — the supremacy of Vishnu — as the essential 'handle.'
how_to_reach: Direct trains to Puri; ~60 km by road from Bhubaneswar.

significance: One of the jyotirlingas; the linga is white like a mallika flower with the moon in Shiva's matted locks. Worship of Rudra here and a bath in the Devahrada yields merit equal to an Ashvamedha yaga.
how_to_reach: Road from Hyderabad (~200 km), Kurnool or Nandyal; buses to Srisailam hill.

significance: Where Narasimha manifested to slay Hiranyakashipu and protect Prahlada; Vadiraja dwells on the paradoxical man-lion form as a mark of the Lord's transcendent, omnipresent nature.
how_to_reach: Rail to Nandyal (~65 km), then road to Lower and Upper Ahobilam.

deity: Sacred river; waters used for Narasimha's puja
significance: The river at Ahobilam whose waters are used for the worship of Narasimha; invoked as washing the deity's lotus feet and thereby purifying the devotee's sins.
how_to_reach: At Ahobilam; reach via Nandyal then road.

significance: A confluence of seven rivers (including Krishnaveni, Malapahari, Bhimarathi, Tunga, Bhadra, Bhavanashini) where human doshas are removed and auspiciousness bestowed; now largely submerged by the Srisailam reservoir, visible only seasonally.
how_to_reach: Road from Kurnool (~30 km); seasonal access.

significance: The Tunga and Bhadra, said to originate from the tusks of Varaha, are sweet-watered rivers that destroy heaps of sins and form a path to moksha; they meet at Koodli in Shivamogga district.
how_to_reach: Accessed at various points; Hospet/Harihar/Koodli by road and rail.

significance: Capital region of the 16th-century Vijayanagara empire; the Vijaya Vittala temple is celebrated and Pampa is revered as destroying sins by merely uttering its name. The Virupaksha temple is where Sri Vyasaraja composed the Shivastuti; the Vittala shrine was later damaged after Talikota.
how_to_reach: Rail to Hosapete (~13 km), then road to Hampi.

deity: Hanuman's birthplace; Navavrindavana of Dvaita saints
significance: An early Vijayanagara capital and, in Madhwa tradition, the birthplace of Hanuman; nearby Navavrindavana holds the vrindavanas of nine Dvaita yatis (including Jayatirtha and Vyasatirtha). Vadiraja likens eight of them to the eight diggajas guarding Madhwa siddhanta.
how_to_reach: Rail to Hosapete, then road; cross the Tungabhadra near Hampi.

significance: One of the swayamvyakta maha-kshetras and 'Vaikuntha on earth,' attested in the Vedas, Pancharatra and over twelve Puranas (chiefly the Venkatesha Mahatmya). The hill is a manifestation of Shesha, and Swami Pushkarini is its foremost tank.
how_to_reach: Rail to Tirupati, then road/bus (or walk) up the ghat to Tirumala.

significance: The golden-hued river is invoked to make the pilgrim pure and grant a golden radiance of face; the famous Srikalahasti temple stands on its banks.
how_to_reach: Rail to Srikalahasti / Renigunta; road from Tirupati (~35 km).

significance: Named in the Suvarnamukhi passage as the 'famous' temple on the river's banks; referenced within the Tirtha Prabandha's Suvarnamukhi verse rather than as a standalone entry.
how_to_reach: Rail to Srikalahasti; road from Tirupati (~35 km).

significance: Vadiraja celebrates Varadaraja, who appeared from the middle of Brahma's yajna-vedika; Kanchi is figured as the girdle (kanchi) of Bhudevi. He also notes the Ekamreshwara linga at the mango-tree root and the Kamakshi shrine.
how_to_reach: Rail to Kanchipuram; road from Chennai (~75 km).

significance: The Arunachala hill is held to embody the agni-tattva linga of Shiva; the text notes the auspicious Kartika Pournami fire lit atop the hill.
how_to_reach: Rail to Tiruvannamalai; road from Chennai (~180 km) via Vellore.

significance: Per the sthala purana, where Vamana took the Trivikrama form and measured the whole brahmanda with the tip of his toe-nail; the temple has an unusually tall (~10 ft) Trivikrama murti.
how_to_reach: Road from Villupuram (~35 km) or Tiruvannamalai.

significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam where, per the sthala purana, Shiva appeared to bless a rishi; presented as a sacred kshetra ~60 km from Tirukoilur.
how_to_reach: Rail to Vriddhachalam; road from Tirukoilur (~60 km).

significance: Among the eight swayamvyakta kshetras; where Varaha incarnated to slay Hiranyaksha and, after rescuing Bhudevi, took residence. Sri Madhwacharya performed a chaturmasya here, and a carved image of Madhwa on a temple pillar is worshipped to this day.
how_to_reach: Road from Chidambaram (~25 km) or Vriddhachalam.

significance: One of the most famous tirtha-kshetras of South India, dense with temples; its five principal shrines are Sharangapani, Kumbheshwara, Vageeshwara, Ramaswamy and Chakrapani.
how_to_reach: Rail to Kumbakonam; road from Thanjavur (~40 km).

deity: Ranganatha (Vishnu on Shesha, with Sri and Bhudevi)
significance: One of the self-manifested (svayam-vyakta) shrines of Vishnu, with seven concentric prakaras. The commentary recounts the deity was given by Brahma to Ikshvaku, entrusted by Rama to Vibhishana, and remained here through King Dharmavarma's merit.
how_to_reach: On Srirangam island in the Kaveri, ~10 km from Tiruchirappalli; rail/road via Trichy.

modern_name: Sacred tank, fifth prakara of Srirangam temple
significance: Chandra performed tapas here after leaving the Ganga in Shiva's hair, so his sannidhana at this tirtha is exceptionally strong; the commentary says only an unfortunate person would fail to worship Chandra here.
how_to_reach: Within the Srirangam temple complex (fifth enclosure).

deity: Associated with Ranganatha on its river-islands
significance: 'The mother of the people of Chola desha' and 'the giver of both bhukti and mukti'; Ranganatha is enshrined on the islands where the river splits and rejoins at the three Ranga-kshetras. Celebrated in the Vedas, Mahabharata and Bhagavata.
how_to_reach: Flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; sacred bathing points at the Ranga-kshetras.

significance: Yama performed intense tapas at this hill to obtain the darshan of Narayana as Sundararaja; the deity is likened to the shining moon adorning the sacred hill.
how_to_reach: ~20 km northeast of Madurai in the Alagar Hills.

deity: Associated with Vishnu (from the Lord's anklet/nupura)
significance: At Vrushabhachala; said to have issued from the Lord's anklet. Vadiraja invokes its waters to relieve him from 'the slush of the hard group of sins' and to sanctify the heart.
how_to_reach: At/near Alagar Koil, ~20 km from Madurai.

deity: Rama (two-armed reclining form on darbha grass)
significance: Where Rama lay on a bed of kusha (darbha) grass awaiting the ocean's permission to cross to Lanka — the same grass he had once turned into a weapon to protect Sita; the commentary also links the site with Vibhishana's surrender.
how_to_reach: Near Ramanathapuram, en route to Rameswaram.

modern_name: Rama Setu (shoals between Dhanushkodi and Sri Lanka)
significance: The bridge built by the vanara army is extolled as a 'touchstone' generating faith in Rama's glory; the ocean's tides are pictured as rising in devotion at each stone that bears the dust of Rama's feet.
how_to_reach: Reached from Rameswaram / Dhanushkodi at the southeastern tip of Pamban island.

deity: Shiva as Rameshwara (linga established by Rama)
significance: Among the four greatest pilgrimage sites of Bharata (with Dwaraka, Badari and Puri). The commentary argues Rama installed the linga for lokashikshana (public instruction), not to expiate sin — since Rama himself destroys all sin and Shiva meditates on the Rama-mantra.
how_to_reach: On Pamban island, connected by the Pamban rail/road bridge from Mandapam.

significance: Citing the Skanda Purana, Rama broke the Setu here with the reverse tip of his bow to reassure Vibhishana; visiting is said to grant merit equal to bathing at numerous tirthas.
how_to_reach: ~20 km beyond Rameswaram at the eastern tip of Pamban island.

significance: The Tamraparni bestows moksha, illustrated by the image that 'even a shell in that river gives liberation to the water fallen into it' (i.e. produces pearls); its waters increase bhakti toward Hari.
how_to_reach: Flows through the Tirunelveli region of southern Tamil Nadu.

significance: The launch point of Hanuman's leap to Lanka; the force of his leap is said to have sunk most of the mountain into the earth, reframed as the mountain descending to carry to Bhudevi the assurance that Hanuman had reached Sita.
how_to_reach: Peak near the Kanyakumari–Tirunelveli border (note: some traditions place Hanuman's Mahendragiri in Odisha).

significance: At the southern tip of Bharata where three seas meet; the Devi grants wealth, health and moksha. She took the form of a virgin (kanya) to slay the demon Bana, who could be killed only by a maiden. Madhvacharya visited on his southern tour; Agastya did tapas nearby.
how_to_reach: Southernmost tip of the Indian mainland; rail terminus at Kanyakumari.

significance: The name derives from the tradition that Indra was purified here after Gautama Muni's curse; the commentary draws a moral that purifying an ordinary helpless person's mind yields greater merit than purifying even a powerful deity like Indra.
how_to_reach: ~10–13 km from Kanyakumari, near Nagercoil.

deity: Adi Kesava Perumal (Vishnu reclining, Anantashayana form)
significance: A reclining form of the Lord described as flawless and 'the ocean of all auspicious attributes'; the very large murti (~18 ft) is viewed through three doorways, with a slain demon placed near the Lord's feet — parallel to Padmanabha.
how_to_reach: ~20 km from Thiruvananthapuram / ~30 km from Nagercoil, in Kanyakumari district.

significance: Symbolizes the destruction of sins through knowledge: like ghee (ghrta) feeding a flame, its waters are the 'root cause in lighting the fire of perfect knowledge' that burns away ignorance, granting jnana to bathers.
how_to_reach: Near Anantashayana (Thiruvananthapuram).

deity: Vishnu as Ananta Padmanabha (reclining on Shesha)
significance: The Lord's reclining posture shows His infinite power in effortlessly governing the universe; the enormous murti is viewed through three doors (feet, mid-body, face), linked by the commentary to the Taittiriya Upanishad. Madhvacharya visited on his southern pilgrimage. Concluding kshetra of the section.
how_to_reach: In Thiruvananthapuram city; ~85 km from Kanyakumari.
